summary: For ages 6–7: count to 120 starting from ANY number below 120, and read/write numerals to 120. Two skills carry the load: (i) counting on from an arbitrary start (not always from 1), so children feel the count as a movable sequence they can enter anywhere; and (ii) crossing 100 — reading and writing 100–120, where the hundreds place appears and children must learn that 'one hundred and eight' is 108, not 1008. Give special attention to the 99→100 and 109→110 crossings and to the write-what-you-hear trap. The primary approach is an interactive 120-grid twinned with a number line; a static grid and short written/spoken checks are useful supporting tools with their own limits.
misconceptions: Writing three-digit words literally: 'one hundred and eight' → 1008, or 'one hundred and fifteen' → 10015/1015 (missing the zero-tens placeholder or concatenating).
Stalling or resetting at 100 (saying 'one hundred, two hundred' or restarting at 1) when counting on.
Only being able to count from 1, not from an arbitrary start number.
Reading 108 as 'ten eight' or 'one-oh-eight' without the hundred meaning.

activities.title: Count on from any number across 100 (interactive grid and line)
steps: Pick any starting number — for example 47, 96, or 112 — and count on out loud, one number at a time, as each number is highlighted in turn on a 120-grid and a matching number line.

Deliberately practise starts that sit just before a boundary (start at 96 and count 97, 98, 99, 100, 101; start at 108 and count 109, 110, 111) so the century and decade rollovers get extra rehearsal.
Count backwards too (for example from 112 down past 100) to show the sequence runs both ways across the boundary.
While counting, keep the single running count going — avoid resetting to 1 or jumping to 'two hundred' after 100.
activities.insight: The count is a movable window you can enter at any number, not a fixed chant that must start at 1; it continues smoothly past 100, where 101–120 are 'one hundred and ...'.

activities.title: Build the numeral from the spoken words with place-value cards
steps: Hear or read a number word such as 'one hundred and eight' and build it with place-value / arrow cards: pull the '100' card, note there are zero tens, then the '8' card, so the cards overlay to read 108.
Say what job the 0 is doing in 108 — it holds the empty tens place.
Do the same for 'one hundred and fifteen' → compose 100, then 1 ten, then 5, reading 115.
Confront the trap directly: write the words out literally (1008, 10015) and compare that number to where it would sit relative to the 120-grid — far off the board — to see why it can't be right.
activities.insight: Three-digit numerals are built by place value, not by stringing the spoken words together; the zero in 108 is a tens placeholder, and concatenating words gives numbers far too large.

activities.title: Fluency and trap checks: sequence, read, and write across 100
steps: Fill the missing numbers in a run that crosses the boundary, e.g. 97, 98, __, __, 101.
Read a given numeral aloud, e.g. 108, as 'one hundred and eight'.
Write the numeral for a spoken/written number word, e.g. 'one hundred and fifteen' → 115.
Use a slider or marker to land on target numbers up to 120.
activities.insight: These checks show whether a learner can complete sequences across 100, read numerals 100–120 with their hundred meaning, and write them by place value rather than concatenating words; sustained counting across 100 is confirmed through the spoken counting activity.

activities.title: 120-grid as a reference map
steps: Explore a 120-grid, tapping cells to hear and see each numeral, with 101–120 displayed as 'one hundred and ...'.
Trace the pattern down each column and across each row to see how the sequence continues past 100 just as it did below it.
Point to where 99, 100, 109 and 110 sit and name them.
activities.insight: The counting pattern continues unbroken past 100, and 101–120 keep the same ones/tens pattern with 'one hundred and ...' in front.

checkQuestion: Watch counting and writing across 100. 'Count on from 97 up past 110 for me. Read this: 108. Now write “one hundred and fifteen” as a numeral.' Watch the century rollover and the placeholder zero in 108.
checkAnswer: Counts 97, 98, 99, 100, 101 … 110, 111 … without stalling; reads 108 as 'one hundred and eight'; writes 115.
